passage: Rehana failed her cost accounting paper, and for two weeks she didn't stop asking why. In the hostel room in Lucknow, she'd lie on the bed going over it: was it the night before, when she couldn't sleep? Was she just bad at numbers? Did it mean she'd chosen the wrong course, the wrong life? Every answer led to another question. Zainab, her roommate, tried to help. "Want to look at the paper together and see which questions went wrong?" "Not yet," Rehana said. "I need to understand why first." The re-exam form sat on her desk, unfilled. Her tea went cold every evening. She felt as if she was thinking very hard, getting nowhere, and getting heavier.

qa.q: What sat on Rehana's desk, unfilled?
qa.a: The re-exam form.

qa.q: Why does Rehana say "I need to understand why first"?
qa.a: Rehana feels anxious and stuck, and searching for the cause feels responsible, as if a plan can't come until she knows what the failure says about her.

qa.q: What small step could break Rehana's loop?
qa.a: Accepting Zainab's offer to go through the paper question by question and filling in the re-exam form, turning "why" into "what next".

qa.q: How might Zainab feel when the offer is put off?
qa.a: Zainab may feel helpless and worried, watching a friend sink further while a practical way forward sits unused.

grounding: A student who failed a paper keeps asking why and what it means about her, without making any plan, and her mood sinks.

"Thinking, bhaiya."
Hemant sat at the foot of his younger brother's bed. "About the maths paper?"
"About why I failed it. Was it the new professor? Was it me? Maybe I'm just not an engineering person. Maybe I never was, and Papa pushed me, and I went along, and now..."

"For the supplementary. It's in six weeks."

passage: After I failed Organic Chemistry II last semester, I spent a whole month inside one question: why? I'd lie awake building theories. Maybe I wasn't smart enough. Maybe I'd been lucky in first year and this was the truth coming out. Maybe something was wrong with how my brain worked. Each theory made me feel worse, but I kept at it, because it felt like work, like I was being responsible. Sarika, my lab partner, finally asked, "Lavanya, after all this thinking, what are you going to do differently?" I opened my mouth and nothing came out. I had a hundred reasons and not one plan. That night I wrote three: office hours every week, practice reaction problems daily, redo the paper with Sarika. The why can wait. I feel lighter already.

qa.q: What three steps did Lavanya write that night?
qa.a: Office hours every week, practice reaction problems daily, and redo the paper with Sarika.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya keep building theories even though each made things worse?
qa.a: It felt like responsible work, as if understanding the cause had to come first, so stopping seemed careless.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Sarika asking what Lavanya would do differently; it exposed a hundred reasons but no plan, and led to three concrete steps.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel being part of the plan?
qa.a: Sarika may feel glad that the question helped, and happy to redo the paper together as a partner.

grounding: A student stuck asking why the paper was failed realises the thinking has no plan, and writes concrete steps.

Mentor notes, Jomon Kurian, B.Sc Nursing first year, 18 September
Seema came to my cabin again today, the third time since the anatomy results. She failed the paper by six marks. She doesn't ask what to do about the supplementary exam. She asks why. "Was it the hostel noise? Am I too slow? Maybe I'm not made for nursing, sir." Each visit brings the same questions in a new order, and she leaves looking more tired, not less. She told me she lies awake going over the question paper line by line.
Today I didn't answer the why. I asked her to write down one thing she could do this week. She sat with the pen a long time, then wrote: "Ask Rincy to study the bones chapter with me on Tuesday." I've asked her to come back on Friday and tell me how it went.

Friday, 11:40 p.m.
Results came out at noon. Failed Business Law. 31.
I've spent the whole day on one question. Why? Was it the two weeks I gave to the college fest? Was it that I read the cases but never practised writing answers? Or am I just someone who can't handle serious subjects, and everyone was being nice about it until now? Maybe Abba was right that I should have taken science.
Round and round on the bus, in the canteen, in the shower. Every answer I find makes me feel worse, and none of them tell me what to do.
Thomas texted at 9: "reval or supplementary? need help making a plan?" I typed "idk" and put the phone face down.
Still awake. Still asking why.
Noor

A Monday in May. Vikas saw the result online: failed in thermodynamics. He sat on his hostel bed. Why? Why? He went over every day of the exam week. His roommate Harsha asked if he wanted food. He shook his head.

The Thursday after. Vikas was still in the same loop. Was it the professor? Was he just not engineering material? Did it prove his father was right to doubt him? He made no notes, opened no book. Harsha found him staring at the ceiling at noon. "Have you checked when the re-exam is?" "Not yet. I'm trying to understand why it happened."

Two weeks later, a Tuesday. The re-exam form deadline had passed. Vikas still didn't have an answer to why. He hadn't found out what he got wrong. He felt worse than on the first day. Harsha sat beside him. "Why won't help now. What will you do?" Vikas had no answer.

qa.q: What subject did Vikas fail?
qa.a: Thermodynamics.

qa.q: Why did Vikas keep asking why instead of acting?
qa.a: He felt that understanding the cause would help, but the loop only deepened his low mood and self-doubt, and he felt stuck.

qa.q: What could Vikas do now, even after missing the re-exam form?
qa.a: He could ask the department about the next exam, get the marked paper to see what went wrong, and talk to a counsellor about the low mood.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel watching Vikas stay stuck?
qa.a: Harsha may feel worried and helpless, trying to nudge Vikas toward action but seeing no change.

Sarita, you think you're the first one to fail an exam? Come, let me tell you about your Manoj mama.

Second year of engineering, I failed Fluid Mechanics. Thirty-one out of a hundred. I came back to the hostel and lay on the bed and asked the ceiling, why? Why me? Was I stupid? Had my father wasted his money? My roommate Gopal went to dinner, came back, and I was still asking the same questions. For two weeks I did that. I didn't open a single book. I felt worse every day.

Then Gopal threw the question paper on my chest. "Stop asking why. Circle the questions you couldn't do." I circled six. Four were from the same chapter I'd skipped.

That's all. A chapter, not my whole worth. I cleared the supplementary in October. So, Sarita beta, which chapter did you skip?

The hostel Wi-Fi died on the evening the results came out, so Lalremsiami had to walk to the library in the rain to see the screen: Statistics, Fail.

Back in the room, wet socks still on, she couldn't stop. Why did this happen? Was it the late nights? Was she just bad at numbers? Did it mean she'd chosen the wrong course? Uma brought her a towel and a plate of rice. Lalremsiami ate two bites and started again: "But why, though?"

For three days the questions ran in circles. She didn't open the notes. She didn't email the professor. The rain didn't stop and neither did the loop, and every round left her feeling heavier.

On the fourth day Uma sat on her bed. "You've asked why maybe a hundred times. Can we ask what now, even once?" Lalremsiami looked at the dripping window for a long time before nodding.

Seema opened her marksheet on a crowded bus in Pune and saw the red line next to Organic Chemistry. For the rest of the week she kept asking herself the same things: why did this happen, why her, what did it say about her.

On Monday she asked while washing dishes. On Tuesday she asked on the terrace. On Wednesday her flatmate Imran found her sitting on the stairs with her earphones in and no music playing.

"Still the chemistry?"

"I just want to understand why."

"Okay. What's the answer so far?"

"That I'm not smart enough. Or I got lazy. Or the paper was unfair. I don't know."

"That's three answers and zero plans," Imran said.

Seema laughed, a little bitterly. She had filled two notebook pages with why and not one line with what next. Her mood hadn't lifted at all since the result.

The organic chemistry result came out on a Monday. I'm Avni, and I got 31 out of 100.
For the next week I thought about almost nothing else. Why did I fail? Was it the mechanisms? The night before, when I only slept four hours? Or is it that I was never cut out for science, and everyone knew but me?
I asked myself this in the bus, at meals, before sleep. Each time I thought I was getting closer to an answer. But I never got to one. I just felt heavier.
Varun, from my lab group, asked on Friday what I was going to do for the supplementary exam. I realised I didn't know. Seven days of thinking, and not one plan.
That frightened me more than the mark. I'd been circling the question like a fan, and the room hadn't cooled at all.

passage:
Hostel mentor's log — Lokesh
Karthik, first-year engineering, failed the mechanics paper. It has been ten days. His roommate asked me to check on him.
He talked for forty minutes. Every sentence was a version of why. "Why did I blank on question three? Why do I always mess up exams? Why did my parents waste money sending me here?" He had clearly been over it hundreds of times. He said, "I need to understand why before I can move on."
He looked tired and flat. He has not opened the mechanics book since the result.
I did not answer the why questions. I asked, "What is one thing you could do this week that would help with the re-exam?" He took a long time. Then he said, "Maybe ask Rao sir for the answer key."
We wrote it down. I will check on Thursday whether he went. If his mood stays this low, I will suggest the college counsellor.
